blocks.text: Eco | from color readouts to management decisions
blocks.attributes: #src-Model-Eco-1 toc="Eco | from color readouts to management decisions" unnumbered

blocks.body: We developed the NemaKlear interactive web app to connect ordinary differential equation (ODE) color simulations, dual-channel density estimation, and economic analysis. Readers can choose simulated soil samples or enter paired absorbance readings, view target nematode density, and compare single-season net returns under different management strategies.

The app lets us directly explore a question: When growers already have the option of uniform treatment, how much additional return can knowledge of nematode density provide? The Eco model therefore connects density with potential yield loss, treatment costs, and testing costs to examine when density information changes management choices and whether that change covers the costs of acquiring information and adjusting treatment.

blocks.text: Exploring the connection from color to returns in the interactive app
blocks.attributes: #src-Model-Eco-4 toc="Exploring the connection from color to returns in the interactive app"

blocks.body: In NemaKlear, readers can follow model outputs through color response → density estimation → management choice → economic outcome.
The app offers two input modes:
**Simulated soil samples:** select samples to observe time-dependent paired color development and corresponding density estimates.
**Manual readings:** enter paired A480 readings for direct density estimation. ODE curves in this mode are shown as references.

After estimating density, the app displays the management tier, potential yield loss, and net-return tables and curves for no testing and no treatment, no testing with uniform treatment, and testing followed by tiered treatment. Readers can compare tiered treatment against both baselines and switch between the density point estimate, prediction-interval endpoints, and adjacent scenarios when tier boundaries are crossed to see how density judgments affect treatment choices.
Three questions guide exploration:
At low densities, can testing help reduce unnecessary treatment?
When tiered and uniform treatment are identical, how does testing cost affect net returns?
At high densities, can additional benefits of intensified treatment cover its added costs?
The app also provides a full report for reviewing parameters and sensitivity analyses and downloading calculations for verification.

blocks.text: Connecting color development and economic analysis through density
blocks.attributes: #src-Model-Eco-15 toc="Connecting color development and economic analysis through density"

blocks.body: The ODE, dual-channel model, and Eco perform three sequential tasks. The ODE describes how receptor input generates color through intracellular pathways; the dual-channel model uses paired color features to estimate southern root-knot nematode density when background nematodes also contribute; Eco combines density estimates with production and management parameters to calculate economic outcomes.
For simulated soil samples, the calculation proceeds as follows:
ODE color output → endpoint absorbance and blank correction → dual-channel density regression → Eco management-scenario comparison.

Density is standardized as second-stage juveniles (J2) per 100 cm³ soil (J2/100 cm³). Paired readings are processed consistently with calibration, and regression results enter Eco after unit and applicability checks. Economic parameters come independently from literature and scenario settings; density connects color and returns.

The interface retains both density point estimates and regression prediction intervals. When an interval crosses a management-tier boundary, the program calculates scenarios on both sides to show possible changes in treatment choices and returns. Negative densities and results outside calibration or economic-model support ranges are not passed downstream; the page explains calibration status and applicability conditions.

blocks.text: Calculating yield loss and net returns from nematode density
blocks.attributes: #src-Model-Eco-21 toc="Calculating yield loss and net returns from nematode density"

blocks.body: We use Spanish protected tomato production and the southern root-knot nematode as an example, calculating returns per hectare per production season from preplanting density.

Density and relative yield are linked by the Seinhorst loss relationship, parameterized from Expósito et al.'s (2020) fit for a spring trial of ungrafted tomato. Below the tolerance level, yield remains normal in the model; above it, relative yield decreases toward a lower limit as density rises. The converted tolerance density in this example is 6 J2/100 cm³, and the minimum relative yield is 0.34。1
The model then incorporates crop selling price, base production cost, treatment cost, and treatment efficacy to calculate:
Single-season net return = sales revenue after residual nematode losses − base production cost − treatment cost − testing cost.

Economic and treatment information follows Talavera-Rubia et al. (2022). 2 We first convert the published population-reduction rate into the fraction of loss avoided using the density–yield relationship at a reference density of 100 J2/100 cm³, then keep that fraction fixed across density scenarios. Thus, a density-independent fraction of loss avoided is a simplifying assumption of this example.

The model combines yield relationships and economic parameters from different studies into a reproducible literature-based scenario. Testing cost is provisionally set to 5 EUR/ha as a team assumption. Sources are retained for published prices, treatment costs, and converted efficacy so these can be updated for actual application conditions.

blocks.text: Using two baselines to distinguish control benefits from information value
blocks.attributes: #src-Model-Eco-28 toc="Using two baselines to distinguish control benefits from information value"

blocks.body: Higher returns after testing can reflect both control itself and density-based treatment adjustment. We therefore define three management scenarios to separate these contributions.
Click the image to view the complete spreadsheet
Tiered treatment follows the preset rules below, with treatment information from reference 2。
Click the image to view the complete spreadsheet

Here, 10 and 80 J2/100 cm³ are preset management-tier boundaries, whereas 6 J2/100 cm³ is the yield curve's tolerance density; they serve different purposes. The model separately compares net returns for candidate strategies to check whether the preset tiers match the highest-return option under current parameters.
We calculate two return differences:

Net-return improvement over no treatment
= net return from testing followed by tiered treatment − net return from no testing and no treatment.

Net-return improvement over uniform treatment
= net return from testing followed by tiered treatment − net return from no testing with uniform treatment.

The first evaluates the entire testing-and-tiered-treatment package; the second evaluates the conditional value of using density information to adjust action when uniform treatment is already available. Separating the baselines helps identify whether increased returns arise from implementing control or changing treatment after obtaining information.

blocks.text: When density information is worth obtaining
blocks.attributes: #src-Model-Eco-40 toc="When density information is worth obtaining"

blocks.body: At a density of 100 J2/100 cm³, with all other parameters at the example settings, the model gives the following results:
Click the image to view the complete spreadsheet

The differences answer distinct questions. The 17,028.48 EUR/ha represents improvement of the full testing-and-control package over no treatment; the 496.26 EUR/ha represents additional net return from adjusting treatment relative to the existing uniform-treatment option. In this scenario, extra losses avoided by stronger treatment cover the additional treatment and testing costs.
The role of information changes with density:
**At low densities,** testing may help reduce unnecessary treatment.
**At intermediate densities,** tiered and uniform treatment use the same strategy, and their return difference is −5 EUR/ha, the additional testing cost.
**At high densities,** the value of intensified treatment depends on whether extra avoided losses cover added costs.
Evaluating detection value therefore requires examining both whether density information changes management choices and whether those changes improve net returns 。

We further varied testing cost, treatment cost, treatment efficacy, and crop selling price separately to examine sensitivity of both return differences. When tiered and uniform treatment use the same measure, shared cost and efficacy parameters change together to maintain consistent comparison conditions.

blocks.label: Evidence and limitations
blocks.body: These are conditional calculations under specified density, cost, and efficacy assumptions. Current density prediction intervals reflect formal uncertainty in simulated regression; empirical coverage still requires real samples and readout calibration. Interval endpoints and adjacent-density scenarios illustrate economic effects of altered judgments; the resulting return range is not a confidence interval for returns. Real detection errors may change treatment choices, and their economic effects require evaluation against measured error distributions.

blocks.text: Feeding economic comparisons back into detection design
blocks.attributes: #src-Model-Eco-52 toc="Feeding economic comparisons back into detection design"

blocks.body: Eco focuses detection design on density ranges where management choices may change. Semiquantitative or quantitative information can support management tiers when different densities imply different treatments. Near boundaries, estimation bias may alter choices, making these ranges priorities for calibration and evaluation.

The app reflects this need by retaining density estimates, corresponding management tiers, and return comparisons against both baselines, while showing adjacent scenarios when estimated ranges cross tier boundaries. This helps readers judge the dependence of conclusions on density estimates.

We will calibrate density estimates using real samples and smartphone readouts and update sampling coverage, per-hectare testing costs, and management parameters through application research. These data will test whether readouts distinguish relevant density ranges and whether obtaining that information is affordable.

For reproducibility and updates, parameter configurations are stored separately from calculation code, with example inputs and regenerable reports. Existing automated checks cover density–loss calculations, cost accounting, and consistency of comparison baselines; real application benefits still require local validation. Other researchers can replace crops, prices, and treatment parameters to assess their detection systems under specific management conditions.
